```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6)
```

## Overview

`ssGSEA3.0` runs single-sample Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (ssGSEA) on gene-centric
expression data, and PTM-Signature Enrichment Analysis (PTM-SEA) on site-centric
phosphoproteomics data scored against the directional
[PTM signatures database (PTMsigDB)](https://proteomics.broadapps.org/ptmsigdb/).
Significance is assessed via a gene-level bootstrap, replacing the gene-label
permutation testing used by the original `ssGSEA2.0`.

This vignette:

1. explains *why* that replacement happened,
2. walks through two ordinary ssGSEA analyses on the same tumor NMF factors --
   against the curated HALLMARK collection, and against the much larger and more
   functionally diverse REACTOME pathway collection -- and
3. walks through a directional PTM-SEA analysis (a phosphoproteomics perturbation
   dataset vs. PTMsigDB), comparing the result to the original `ssGSEA2.0`.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(ssGSEA3)
```

## Why bootstrap instead of permutation?

### A known problem with weighted scoring under permutation

`ssGSEA2.0`'s significance testing permuted gene labels to build a null distribution
for each gene set's enrichment score. This works cleanly when every gene contributes
equally to the score (`weight = 0`), but is known to produce badly miscalibrated
p-values whenever the score is weighted by actual expression magnitude
(`weight > 0`) -- documented as GitHub issue #45 against the original `ssGSEA2.0`
repository. Testing purely random, biologically meaningless gene sets at
`weight = 0.75` gave a mean p-value of about 0.001 (i.e. almost always called
"significant") instead of the ~0.5 expected under a true null.

An informal fix -- stop reordering the correlation vector along with the permuted
gene ranks -- corrected that calibration problem, but at a real cost: on a real
PI3K-perturbation dataset, the same fix reduced detection of expected cell-cycle
pathways at `weight = 0.75` from 6/14 down to 0/14 at 6 hours, and from 10/14 down
to 3/14 at 24 hours. Fixing the false-positive problem this way also suppressed real
signal -- a fundamental validity-vs-power tension that a purely permutation-based
approach could not resolve.

`ssGSEA3.0` circumvents the need for this tradeoff by using bootstrap sampling. In a
traditional permutation test, random permutations of the data are used to derive the
null distribution, and the p-value is calculated based on how extreme the observed
value is compared to the null distribution. Here, we use bootstrap sampling to
determine the standard deviation of the observed value, and the p-value is determined
akin to a z-test on the observed value (using the bootstrap-derived standard
deviation). The effective null distribution is the mean shifted bootstrap values. With
this approach, all gene-gene relationships and dependencies are maintained, with the
bootstrap providing a perturbation of the enrichment score, thereby minimizing bias and
controlling false positives.

### Directional (PTM-SEA) scoring gets an extra benefit

PTM-SEA's directional gene sets (with `;u`/`;d`-labeled "up" and "down" members)
benefit from bootstrap resampling in a second, independent way. Permutation always
preserves the exact up/down membership counts of a gene set, only ever moving
*where* they fall in the ranking. Bootstrap resampling with replacement lets some
members drop out (and others duplicate) in any given replicate, so the up- and
down-regulated counts genuinely vary from replicate to replicate -- a richer,
two-sided source of resampling variability with no permutation-based analogue.

A controlled simulation with known ground truth (embedding a real, moderate,
correctly-oriented effect) confirmed this: both methods are well-calibrated under a
true null, but bootstrap shows a real, statistically robust power advantage
specifically for directional scoring (McNemar p = 0.0001, odds ratio 1.85) that
does not replicate for non-directional scoring at the same sample size. The two
worked examples below show both regimes on real data.

## Example 1: ssGSEA on tumor NMF factors

The bundled example is a PANOPLY LUAD (lung adenocarcinoma) NMF factorization
(4 factors, CPTAC/ICPC v6.1) scored against the MSigDB HALLMARK collection --
an ordinary (non-directional) ssGSEA analysis.

```{r luad-score, eval = FALSE}
res <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = "example/LUAD_matrix_W_combined_signed_gc.gct",
  output.prefix = "luad",
  gene.set.databases = "db/msigdb/h.all.v7.0.symbols.gmt",
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 1, correl.type = "z.score",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 10, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

```{r luad-load}
## the call above takes ~30 min at the default nperm=1000 -- loading its
## precomputed output here keeps this vignette's own build fast, and keeps
## the displayed results consistent with the full-nperm comparison below
## (rather than a faster-but-different reduced-nperm run)
res <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "luad_ssgsea3_result.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"))
res
```

The four factors are labeled by their NMF cluster number; renaming them to their
published biological identities makes the heatmap self-explanatory:

```{r luad-rename}
cluster.names <- c(
  "1" = "Unstable-proliferative", "2" = "Quiescent-EGFR",
  "3" = "Immune-active-KRAS", "4" = "Stable-early-stage"
)

rename_cols <- function(x, map) {
  colnames(x) <- unname(map[colnames(x)])
  x
}
res$scores <- rename_cols(res$scores, cluster.names)
res$pvalues <- rename_cols(res$pvalues, cluster.names)
res$fdr <- rename_cols(res$fdr, cluster.names)
res$sample.names <- unname(cluster.names[res$sample.names])
```

```{r luad-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 10}
ht <- plot_ssgsea_heatmap(res, top_n = 10, fdr.max = 0.05,
                           title = "LUAD PANOPLY -- HALLMARK (ssGSEA3.0)")
ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht)
```

The proliferation program (`MYC_TARGETS`, `E2F_TARGETS`, `MTORC1_SIGNALING`,
`OXIDATIVE_PHOSPHORYLATION`, `GLYCOLYSIS`) is strongly and specifically enriched in
the "Unstable-proliferative" factor, matching its published biological identity --
a useful sanity check that the scoring and reporting pipeline agree with the
underlying biology.

### Comparison against the original ssGSEA2.0

This dataset is scored at `weight = 1` -- exactly the regime affected by the
weight-dependent calibration issue described above, so it demonstrates the
*other* side of the bootstrap's benefit: rather than finding more real signal
(as in the directional PTM-SEA example below), it trims down some of the
original ssGSEA2.0's likely-inflated calls while retaining the large majority
of them. As above, these are precomputed results (`nperm = 1000`, run outside
this vignette):

```{r luad-comparison}
cmp.luad <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "luad_ssgsea2_vs_ssgsea3_comparison.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"
))
nes2.luad <- as.vector(cmp.luad$ssgsea2.nes)
nes3.luad <- as.vector(cmp.luad$ssgsea3.nes)

cat("Gene sets compared:", length(cmp.luad$gene.set.names), "\n")
cat("NES Pearson r:    ", round(cor(nes2.luad, nes3.luad), 3), "\n")
cat("NES Spearman rho: ", round(cor(nes2.luad, nes3.luad, method = "spearman"), 3), "\n")

## a gene set counts as "significant" if FDR<0.05 in >=1 of the 4 samples --
## NOT the same as counting gene-set x sample cells, which would double-count
## any gene set significant in multiple samples
sig2.luad <- apply(cmp.luad$ssgsea2.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
sig3.luad <- apply(cmp.luad$ssgsea3.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
cat("\nGene sets significant (FDR < 0.05 in >=1 sample), of", length(cmp.luad$gene.set.names), "total:\n")
cat("  ssGSEA2.0:", sum(sig2.luad), " ssGSEA3.0:", sum(sig3.luad),
    " both:", sum(sig2.luad & sig3.luad), " ssGSEA2.0-only:", sum(sig2.luad & !sig3.luad),
    " ssGSEA3.0-only:", sum(!sig2.luad & sig3.luad), "\n")
```

```{r luad-scatter, fig.height = 5}
plot(nes2.luad, nes3.luad,
     xlab = "ssGSEA2.0 NES", ylab = "ssGSEA3.0 NES", pch = 16, col = "#00000066",
     main = "LUAD PANOPLY, HALLMARK: NES agreement")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

`ssGSEA3.0` agrees with `ssGSEA2.0` on the overwhelming majority of significant
calls (`r sum(sig2.luad & sig3.luad)` shared), while dropping
`r sum(sig2.luad & !sig3.luad)` calls unique to `ssGSEA2.0` and adding almost
none of its own -- consistent with correcting a false-positive-prone regime
rather than disagreeing with it.

## Example 2: the same tumor NMF factors, scored against REACTOME

HALLMARK's 50 gene sets are curated to be similarly sized and mechanistically
narrow (one canonical process each). REACTOME is far larger and more
functionally diverse -- gene sets range from a handful of genes up to several
hundred, spanning everything from individual metabolic reactions to broad
pathway categories -- which makes it a useful second, harder test of the same
LUAD data: does `ssGSEA3.0` agree with `ssGSEA2.0` as well on a
size/function-heterogeneous database as it does on a curated, uniform one?

```{r luad-reactome-score, eval = FALSE}
res.reactome <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = "example/LUAD_matrix_W_combined_signed_gc.gct",
  output.prefix = "luad_reactome",
  gene.set.databases = "db/msigdb/reactome_subset.gmt",
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 1, correl.type = "z.score",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 10, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

```{r luad-reactome-load}
## as above, loading the precomputed output instead of re-running the ~30
## min scoring call live -- restricted to the 1,167 gene sets common to
## both engines being compared below
res.reactome <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "luad_reactome_ssgsea3_result.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"
))
res.reactome
```

```{r luad-reactome-rename}
res.reactome$scores <- rename_cols(res.reactome$scores, cluster.names)
res.reactome$pvalues <- rename_cols(res.reactome$pvalues, cluster.names)
res.reactome$fdr <- rename_cols(res.reactome$fdr, cluster.names)
res.reactome$sample.names <- unname(cluster.names[res.reactome$sample.names])
```

Auto-selecting top terms by `|NES|` on a size-heterogeneous database like
REACTOME tends to surface a handful of very large "umbrella" gene sets (e.g.
`METABOLISM_OF_RNA`, `CELL_CYCLE`) rather than the mechanistically specific
pathways a reader would actually want to see. Instead, this heatmap uses a
curated list of 30 lung adenocarcinoma driver pathways spanning EGFR/ERBB,
RAS/RAF/MAPK, ALK, PI3K/AKT, WNT, NOTCH, TGF-beta, TP53, DNA damage/repair,
cell-cycle checkpoints, apoptosis, KEAP1-NRF2, telomere maintenance, FGFR,
MET, and hypoxia/VEGF signaling:

```{r luad-reactome-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 10}
luad.driver.pathways <- c(
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_EGFR", "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_EGFR_IN_CANCER",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_ERBB4", "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_ALK_IN_CANCER",
  "REACTOME_REGULATION_OF_RAS_BY_GAPS", "REACTOME_SIGNALLING_TO_ERKS",
  "REACTOME_MAP2K_AND_MAPK_ACTIVATION",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_MODERATE_KINASE_ACTIVITY_BRAF_MUTANTS",
  "REACTOME_PI3K_AKT_SIGNALING_IN_CANCER",
  "REACTOME_CONSTITUTIVE_SIGNALING_BY_ABERRANT_PI3K_IN_CANCER",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_WNT_IN_CANCER", "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_NOTCH4",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_TGF_BETA_RECEPTOR_COMPLEX",
  "REACTOME_SMAD2_SMAD3_SMAD4_HETEROTRIMER_REGULATES_TRANSCRIPTION",
  "REACTOME_REGULATION_OF_TP53_ACTIVITY",
  "REACTOME_REGULATION_OF_TP53_ACTIVITY_THROUGH_PHOSPHORYLATION",
  "REACTOME_TP53_REGULATES_TRANSCRIPTION_OF_DNA_REPAIR_GENES",
  "REACTOME_G1_S_DNA_DAMAGE_CHECKPOINTS", "REACTOME_G2_M_DNA_DAMAGE_CHECKPOINT",
  "REACTOME_MITOTIC_SPINDLE_CHECKPOINT", "REACTOME_APOPTOSIS",
  "REACTOME_KEAP1_NFE2L2_PATHWAY", "REACTOME_NUCLEAR_EVENTS_MEDIATED_BY_NFE2L2",
  "REACTOME_TELOMERE_MAINTENANCE", "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_FGFR",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_FGFR_IN_DISEASE", "REACTOME_CELLULAR_RESPONSE_TO_HYPOXIA",
  "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_VEGF", "REACTOME_SIGNALING_BY_MET",
  "REACTOME_DISEASES_OF_DNA_REPAIR"
)
ht.reactome <- plot_ssgsea_heatmap(res.reactome, terms = luad.driver.pathways,
                                    fdr.max = 0.05,
                                    title = "LUAD PANOPLY -- REACTOME driver pathways (ssGSEA3.0)")
ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht.reactome)
```

All 30 of these are significant (FDR<0.05) in at least one of the four NMF
factors. Cell-cycle and DNA-damage-checkpoint pathways
(`G1_S_DNA_DAMAGE_CHECKPOINTS`, `TP53_REGULATES_TRANSCRIPTION_OF_DNA_REPAIR_GENES`,
`MITOTIC_SPINDLE_CHECKPOINT`) are strongly and specifically enriched in the
"Unstable-proliferative" factor, matching its published biological identity --
the same kind of biology-matches-label sanity check as the HALLMARK example
above, now visible on a much larger and more heterogeneous database.

### Comparison against the original ssGSEA2.0

As in the HALLMARK example, this dataset is scored at `weight = 1`. REACTOME's
size and functional diversity make the calibration/power tradeoff described
above far more visible than it is on HALLMARK's uniform, curated 50 gene sets:

```{r luad-reactome-comparison}
cmp.reactome <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "luad_reactome_ssgsea2_vs_ssgsea3_comparison.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"
))
nes2.reactome <- as.vector(cmp.reactome$ssgsea2.nes)
nes3.reactome <- as.vector(cmp.reactome$ssgsea3.nes)

cat("Gene sets compared:", length(cmp.reactome$gene.set.names), "\n")
cat("NES Pearson r:    ", round(cor(nes2.reactome, nes3.reactome), 3), "\n")
cat("NES Spearman rho: ", round(cor(nes2.reactome, nes3.reactome, method = "spearman"), 3), "\n")

sig2.reactome <- apply(cmp.reactome$ssgsea2.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
sig3.reactome <- apply(cmp.reactome$ssgsea3.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
cat("\nGene sets significant (FDR < 0.05 in >=1 sample), of", length(cmp.reactome$gene.set.names), "total:\n")
cat("  ssGSEA2.0:", sum(sig2.reactome), " ssGSEA3.0:", sum(sig3.reactome),
    " both:", sum(sig2.reactome & sig3.reactome),
    " ssGSEA2.0-only:", sum(sig2.reactome & !sig3.reactome),
    " ssGSEA3.0-only:", sum(!sig2.reactome & sig3.reactome), "\n")
```

```{r luad-reactome-scatter, fig.height = 5}
plot(nes2.reactome, nes3.reactome,
     xlab = "ssGSEA2.0 NES", ylab = "ssGSEA3.0 NES", pch = 16, col = "#00000022",
     main = "LUAD PANOPLY, REACTOME: NES agreement")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

The pattern is the same shape as HALLMARK's -- `ssGSEA3.0` keeps the large
majority of `ssGSEA2.0`'s significant calls (`r sum(sig2.reactome & sig3.reactome)`
of `r sum(sig2.reactome)`) while adding relatively few new ones of its own
(`r sum(!sig2.reactome & sig3.reactome)`) -- but at much larger absolute scale
(`r length(cmp.reactome$gene.set.names)` gene sets vs. HALLMARK's 50), exactly
as the size/function-diversity hypothesis above predicts: a bigger, more
heterogeneous database makes the same underlying calibration difference
between the two engines far more visible.

## Example 3: PTM-SEA on a PI3K-inhibitor perturbation dataset

The second example (bundled in the package's `example/` directory, alongside
its source) is a site-centric phosphoproteomics dataset from the original
PTM-SEA publication itself (Krug et al. 2019 -- see the package `README` for
the full citation): T47D breast cancer cells treated with the PI3Kα inhibitor
BYL719 (vs. a DMSO control) for 6h and 24h (`PI3K_pert_logP_n2x23936.gct`),
scored against PTMsigDB v2.0.0's flanking-sequence human signatures -- a
directional PTM-SEA analysis. The call is the same shape as the ssGSEA example
above:

```{r ptmsea-score, eval = FALSE}
res.ptmsea <- ssGSEA3(
  input.ds = "example/PI3K_pert_logP_n2x23936.gct",
  output.prefix = "pi3k",
  gene.set.databases = "example/ptm.sig.db.all.flanking.human.v2.0.0.gmt",
  sample.norm.type = "rank", weight = 0, correl.type = "rank",
  statistic = "area.under.RES", min.overlap = 5, nperm = 1000, seed = 42
)
```

```{r ptmsea-load}
## as above, loading the precomputed (nperm=1000) output instead of
## re-running the ~3 hour scoring call live
res.ptmsea <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "pi3k_ssgsea3_result.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"))
res.ptmsea
```

PTMsigDB's `CATEGORY-name` convention (`KINASE-`, `PERT-`, `PATH-`, `DISEASE-`) drives
its own row-grouping in `plot_ssgsea_heatmap()`, distinct from the HALLMARK-category
grouping used above:

```{r ptmsea-heatmap, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 9}
ht.ptmsea <- plot_ssgsea_heatmap(res.ptmsea, top_n = 10, fdr.max = 0.05,
                                  title = "PI3K perturbation -- PTMsigDB v2.0.0 (ssGSEA3.0)")
ComplexHeatmap::draw(ht.ptmsea)
```

### Comparison against the original ssGSEA2.0

Unlike the LUAD comparison above, `weight = 0` is used here deliberately, to
isolate the bootstrap-vs-permutation effect on directional scoring from the
separate weight-dependent issue that comparison demonstrated. The results
below use the default `nperm = 1000` (run outside this vignette, since a full
comparison run against the original, unmodified `ssGSEA2.0` code takes
several hours and depends on software not part of this package):

```{r ptmsea-comparison}
cmp <- readRDS(system.file(
  "extdata", "pi3k_ssgsea2_vs_ssgsea3_comparison.rds", package = "ssGSEA3"
))
nes2 <- as.vector(cmp$ssgsea2.nes)
nes3 <- as.vector(cmp$ssgsea3.nes)
fdr2 <- as.vector(cmp$ssgsea2.fdr)
fdr3 <- as.vector(cmp$ssgsea3.fdr)

cat("Gene sets compared:", length(cmp$gene.set.names), "\n")
cat("NES Pearson r:    ", round(cor(nes2, nes3), 3), "\n")
cat("NES Spearman rho: ", round(cor(nes2, nes3, method = "spearman"), 3), "\n")
cat("FDR Pearson r:    ", round(cor(fdr2, fdr3), 3), "\n")
cat("FDR Spearman rho: ", round(cor(fdr2, fdr3, method = "spearman"), 3), "\n")

## a gene set counts as "significant" if FDR<0.05 in >=1 of the 2 samples --
## NOT the same as counting gene-set x sample cells, which would double-count
## any gene set significant in both samples
sig2 <- apply(cmp$ssgsea2.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
sig3 <- apply(cmp$ssgsea3.fdr < 0.05, 1, any)
cat("\nGene sets significant (FDR < 0.05 in >=1 sample), of", length(cmp$gene.set.names), "total:\n")
cat("  ssGSEA2.0:", sum(sig2), " ssGSEA3.0:", sum(sig3),
    " both:", sum(sig2 & sig3), " ssGSEA2.0-only:", sum(sig2 & !sig3),
    " ssGSEA3.0-only:", sum(!sig2 & sig3), "\n")
```

```{r ptmsea-scatter, fig.height = 5}
plot(nes2, nes3,
     xlab = "ssGSEA2.0 NES", ylab = "ssGSEA3.0 NES", pch = 16, col = "#00000066",
     main = "PI3K perturbation, PTMsigDB v2.0.0: NES agreement")
abline(0, 1, col = "firebrick", lty = 2)
```

`ssGSEA3.0` retains the large majority of `ssGSEA2.0`'s significant calls (`r sum(sig2 & sig3)`
of `r sum(sig2)`) while finding substantially more overall (`r sum(sig3)` vs.
`r sum(sig2)`) -- consistent with the confirmed power advantage for directional
scoring described above, now demonstrated on a real, published dataset.

### Are the additional calls biologically plausible?

A real power advantage should surface signatures that make sense for *this specific*
perturbation, not an arbitrary scattering of unrelated biology. Of the
`r sum(!sig2 & sig3)` signatures significant under `ssGSEA3.0` but never
significant (in either sample) under `ssGSEA2.0`, several sit directly on the
PI3K/AKT/mTOR axis this dataset perturbs:

```{r ptmsea-gained-table}
gained <- c(
  "KINASE-iKiP_PIK3R5", "KINASE-PSP_PDK1/PDPK1", "KINASE-PSP_SGK1",
  "KINASE-PSP_p70S6K/RPS6KB1", "PERT-PSP_TORIN1", "DISEASE-PSP_tuberous_sclerosis"
)
data.frame(
  signature = gained,
  NES_06h = round(cmp$ssgsea3.nes[gained, 1], 2),
  NES_24h = round(cmp$ssgsea3.nes[gained, 2], 2),
  FDR_06h = signif(cmp$ssgsea3.fdr[gained, 1], 2),
  FDR_24h = signif(cmp$ssgsea3.fdr[gained, 2], 2),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

`PIK3R5` is a PI3K regulatory subunit itself; `PDK1` and `SGK1` are AKT-family
kinases immediately downstream of PI3K; `p70S6K` is the canonical mTORC1 output
kinase; `TORIN1` is a PTMsigDB perturbation signature for an mTOR inhibitor;
`tuberous_sclerosis` is a disease signature driven by TSC1/2, a direct mTORC1
regulator. This lines up with the original paper's own reported result for
this exact experiment: PTM-SEA "detected signatures of compounds inhibiting
PI3K as well as targets downstream of PI3K (AKT, MAPK/ERK) covering a
substantial fraction of the PI3K pathway" (Krug et al. 2019). `p70S6K` and
`SGK1`'s substrate signatures moving negative is consistent with declining
mTORC1/AKT-family output as BYL719 inhibition takes hold; `PDK1` and `PIK3R5`
trending positive by 24h instead is consistent with the compensatory
feedback reactivation of upstream RTK/PI3K-node signaling well documented as
a response to PI3K inhibitors specifically (rather than a random, unrelated
direction) -- so even the "wrong-direction" hits are still on-pathway. The
additional calls cluster around the perturbed pathway rather than appearing
as unrelated noise, which is exactly what `ssGSEA2.0` under-detected here.

A related, separate observation: `PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN` -- a PTMsigDB signature
for an *unrelated experiment's* treatment with wortmannin, another PI3K
inhibitor -- was already significant under `ssGSEA2.0` at 24h (FDR
`r signif(cmp$ssgsea2.fdr["PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN", 2], 2)`), so it is not part of
the "newly significant" tally above. But `ssGSEA3.0` closes a near-miss at 6h
(FDR `r signif(cmp$ssgsea2.fdr["PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN", 1], 2)` under `ssGSEA2.0`,
`r signif(cmp$ssgsea3.fdr["PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN", 1], 2)` under `ssGSEA3.0`) and
dramatically strengthens the 24h call (NES
`r round(cmp$ssgsea2.nes["PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN", 2], 1)` to
`r round(cmp$ssgsea3.nes["PERT-PSP_WORTMANNIN", 2], 1)`) -- close to a positive
control for the same PI3K/mTOR-inhibitor resemblance the newly-significant
calls above point to.

## Session info

```{r}
sessionInfo()
```
